title: Chapter LVI

teacherSummary.text: Lady Catherine arrives unexpectedly and demands that Elizabeth promise never to marry Darcy, claiming he is engaged to Anne. Elizabeth refuses to promise anything, defending her right to choose.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LVI,” how does Austen show the great confrontation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LVI develops the idea of the great confrontation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses conflict in Chapter LVI to complicate the reader's understanding of the great confrontation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the great confrontation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the great confrontation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: What gives Elizabeth the courage to defy Lady Catherine? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include dissuaded, upstart, trifled, equipage, patched. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “You are to understand, Miss Bennet, that I came here with the determined resolution of carrying my purpose; nor will I be dissuaded from it.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To advise or exhort against.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Aristocratic marriages were often arranged to keep wealth in families. Now, why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's defiance is a high point of independence against rank. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Conflict, Characterization, Irony.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot conflict, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
